title: DataFrames, Series, and Reading Data
summary: Learn the two core pandas data structures — Series and DataFrame — and how to load tabular data from CSV and Excel files into a DataFrame.

steps.title: Two building blocks: Series and DataFrame
steps.lede: Every pandas table is built from just two structures. Understanding them makes every later operation predictable.

blocks.text: A pandas **Series** is a one-dimensional labeled array that can hold data of any type. Its axis labels are collectively called the **index**. Think of it as a single column of a spreadsheet: each cell has a value, and each row has a label on the left.

A Series can be built from a Python list, a dict, or a scalar. `pd.Series([18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80])` — SwiftDrop delivery times — gets index labels 0 through 6 by default. `pd.Series({"Lagos": 18, "Abuja": 20, "Kano": 22})` uses the dict keys as the index instead.

A pandas **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional labeled data structure whose columns can hold different types. It can be thought of as a dict of Series objects that all share the same index — one Series per column, all aligned row-by-row.

blocks.title: A DataFrame is a collection of Series sharing one index
blocks.alt_text: A DataFrame shown as three columns side by side — order_id, city, delivery_time_minutes — each highlighted as a Series, all sharing the same index (0, 1, 2) on the left.

steps.title: Series and DataFrame from plain Python data
steps.lede: Watch how a list becomes a Series and a dict of lists becomes a DataFrame.

segments.label: A Series built from a Python list: one labelled column of any data type with a default 0, 1, 2 index
segments.summary: Introduces a Series as a one-dimensional labelled array, like a single column in a spreadsheet, using a hallway of numbered apartments as the picture. A short list of three integers becomes a Series with pd.Series. Printing it shows the values in one column, the labels 0, 1, 2 on the left (the index) and the data type underneath. Changing the list to decimals, letters or True/False values changes that type to float, object or bool. It ends by noting the default labels start at 0 and go up by one, and that custom labels can be set.

segments.label: From a dict of lists to a DataFrame: rows, columns, and a single column as a Series
segments.summary: Builds the DataFrame idea in plain Python first: a dict whose keys play the role of columns and whose list values hold the rows. Passing that dict to pd.DataFrame prints a table with an index of 0, 1, 2 on the left. Selecting one column with the same bracket syntax used for a dict key returns a Series, which the presenter describes as one-dimensional, so a DataFrame is a container of several Series that share the index. Working with the index itself is left for a later video.

steps.title: Building a DataFrame and accessing columns
steps.lede: Pass a dict of equal-length lists to pd.DataFrame and use bracket notation to get or set columns.

blocks.text: Pass a dict of equal-length lists to `pd.DataFrame()` and each key becomes a column name: `pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"], "delivery_time_minutes": [18, 20, 22]})` produces a three-column, three-row orders table.

A DataFrame behaves like a dict of like-indexed Series. `orders['city']` returns the city column as a Series. `orders['courier'] = ['Ada', 'Bayo', 'Chidi']` adds a new column — the same bracket syntax you use to read or write a dict entry.

steps.title: Columns and Series
steps.lede: Test your understanding of how DataFrame columns relate to Series.

public.prompt: You have a DataFrame called `orders` with columns `order_id`, `city`, and `delivery_time_minutes`. What is the type of `orders['city']`, and how does it relate to the DataFrame?

options.text: It is a pandas Series that shares the same index as the DataFrame.
It is a Python list extracted from the DataFrame.
It is a new DataFrame containing only the `city` column.
It is a dict mapping index labels to city values.

opt_a.message: Correct. `df['col']` returns a Series — the same one-dimensional, indexed structure that a DataFrame is built from. It shares the DataFrame's index.

opt_b.message: Not quite. `df['col']` uses dict-like syntax, but the result is a pandas Series, not a plain Python list. A Series carries index labels alongside its values.

opt_c.message: A single-column selection with `df['col']` returns a Series, not a DataFrame. To get a one-column DataFrame you would use double brackets: `df[['col']]`.

opt_d.message: A pandas Series is not a dict, even though a DataFrame can be thought of as a dict of Series. `df['city']` returns a Series with an integer index, not a dict.

correct.message: Exactly right. A DataFrame is a collection of like-indexed Series objects, so pulling out a column with `df['col']` gives you back one of those Series.

incorrect.message: Remember: a DataFrame can be thought of as a dict of Series that share an index. Selecting a column with `df['col']` returns one of those Series.

hints: Think about what a DataFrame is made of at its core.
The teaching block said: 'A DataFrame can be treated like a dict of like-indexed Series.'

solution_files.content:
import pandas as pd

# First delivery time (minutes) — change this to test your code
first_time = 18

# Delivery times list — uses first_time as the first element
delivery_times = [first_time, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80]

# Data dict for the DataFrame
data = {
    'order_id': [1001, 1002, 1003],
    'city': ['Lagos', 'Abuja', 'Kano'],
    'delivery_time_minutes': [first_time, 20, 26]
}

# Column to select
col_name = 'delivery_time_minutes'

# Create a Series from delivery_times and print it
s = pd.Series(delivery_times)
print(s)

# Create a DataFrame from data and print it
df = pd.DataFrame(data)
print(df)

# Pull out the col_name column from df and print its type
col = df[col_name]
print(type(col))

tests.message_on_fail: Make sure `df = pd.DataFrame(data)` where `data` has keys `order_id`, `city`, `delivery_time_minutes` with the given lists.
Use `col = df['delivery_time_minutes']` to pull out the column. Its values should match `data['delivery_time_minutes']`.

correct.message: Well done! You built a Series from a list, a DataFrame from a dict of lists, and confirmed that a column pulled from a DataFrame is itself a Series.

incorrect.message: Check that you used `pd.Series(delivery_times)` for the Series, `pd.DataFrame(data)` for the DataFrame, and `df[col_name]` to select the column.

hints: Start with `s = pd.Series(delivery_times)` — pass the list directly.
For the DataFrame, pass the whole `data` dict to `pd.DataFrame()`.

steps.title: Loading CSV and Excel files into a DataFrame
steps.lede: Delivery records often arrive as CSV exports or Excel workbooks. Two pandas functions cover both.

blocks.text: Before pandas can work with your delivery records, you read the file into a DataFrame. `pd.read_csv("orders.csv")` is the main function for reading a delimited text file — such as a CSV — into a DataFrame. `pd.read_excel("orders.xlsx", sheet_name="January")` reads an Excel workbook instead.

`read_csv()` takes the file path (or URL) as its first argument. `read_excel()` additionally takes `sheet_name` to choose which sheet to load — that is why the Excel call names `"January"` but the CSV call does not need to. `read_csv()` also accepts `sep` to change the field delimiter: `pd.read_csv("orders.csv", sep=";")` handles a semicolon-delimited export correctly.

before.code:
# orders.csv — plain text on disk
order_id,city,delivery_time_minutes
1001,Lagos,18
1002,Abuja,20
1003,Kano,22

# Read it into a DataFrame
import pandas as pd
orders = pd.read_csv("orders.csv")

annotations.text: CSV file: comma-separated plain text with a header row
File path is the first argument; pandas infers the header from row 1

after.caption: The DataFrame produced by pd.read_csv("orders.csv") — columns taken from the header row, index added automatically.

blocks.change_summary: pd.read_csv("orders.csv") turns the plain-text CSV on the left into the labeled DataFrame on the right.

steps.title: Choosing the right reader
steps.lede: Which pandas function do you call for a CSV file, and which for an Excel workbook?

public.prompt: A colleague sends you two files: `deliveries.csv` (a comma-separated text file) and `deliveries.xlsx` (an Excel workbook). Which pandas functions do you use to load each file into a DataFrame?

options.text: `pd.read_csv()` for the CSV and `pd.read_excel()` for the Excel file.
`pd.read_excel()` for both, because Excel can also open CSV files.
`pd.read_csv()` for both, because CSV is the universal format.
`pd.read_table()` for the CSV and `pd.read_csv()` for the Excel file.

opt_a.message: Correct. `pd.read_csv()` reads delimited text files like CSV, and `pd.read_excel()` reads Excel workbooks (.xlsx).

opt_b.message: While Excel can open CSV files in the application, `pd.read_excel()` expects a binary Excel workbook format. Use `pd.read_csv()` for `.csv` files.

opt_c.message: `pd.read_csv()` reads delimited text files, not Excel workbooks. Passing an `.xlsx` file to `pd.read_csv()` will raise an error.

opt_d.message: `pd.read_table()` is not the main function taught here, and `pd.read_csv()` does not read Excel workbooks. Use `pd.read_csv()` for CSV and `pd.read_excel()` for `.xlsx`.

correct.message: Right. Each file format has its own reader: `read_csv` for delimited text, `read_excel` for Excel workbooks.

incorrect.message: Each file format needs its own reader. `pd.read_csv()` is for delimited text files like `.csv`; `pd.read_excel()` is for Excel workbooks like `.xlsx`.

hints: The function name matches the file type: `read_csv` for CSV, `read_excel` for Excel.
Think about what each function name describes.

steps.title: Arguments: path, sheet_name, and sep
steps.lede: Test your knowledge of the key arguments for read_csv and read_excel.

public.prompt: A delivery export file uses a semicolon (`;`) as its delimiter instead of a comma. Which call correctly reads it into a DataFrame?

opt_a.message: Correct. `sep=";"` tells `read_csv()` to split fields on semicolons instead of the default comma.

opt_b.message: The argument name is `sep`, not `delimiter` (though `delimiter` is an alias, the value here is wrong: passing `","` keeps the default comma separator, which won't parse a semicolon-delimited file correctly).

opt_c.message: `pd.read_excel()` reads Excel workbooks, not CSV files. The `sheet_name` argument is for Excel sheets, not CSV files.

opt_d.message: Without `sep=";"`, `read_csv()` uses the default comma separator. A semicolon-delimited file would be read as a single column.

correct.message: Exactly. `sep` lets you override the default comma delimiter. The file path is always the first argument.

incorrect.message: When the delimiter is not a comma, pass `sep=";"` (or whatever character is used) as a keyword argument to `pd.read_csv()`.

hints: The default separator for `read_csv` is a comma. What argument changes it?

steps.title: What you've learned
steps.lede: Two structures, two readers — the foundation for every pandas operation ahead.

blocks.text: A **Series** is a one-dimensional labeled array; a **DataFrame** is a collection of Series sharing one index. Pull a column with `df['col']` and you get a Series back. `pd.read_csv()` loads a delimited text file; `pd.read_excel()` loads a workbook. Either way, the result is a DataFrame ready to work with.

remediation_steps.title: Columns are Series — a closer look
remediation_steps.lede: A DataFrame column and a Series are the same thing. Here's the contrast that makes it click.

blocks.text: A **Series** is a one-dimensional labeled array — its labels are the index. A **DataFrame** is a two-dimensional structure you can think of as a dict of Series sharing one index. Every column in a DataFrame is itself a Series.

Use `orders['delivery_time_minutes']` to pull the delivery-time column out of the SwiftDrop orders table. The result is a Series — the same one-dimensional, indexed structure — sharing the DataFrame's index. `orders['courier'] = ['Ada', 'Bayo', 'Chidi']` adds a new column using the same dict-style syntax.

remediation_steps.lede: Two constructors, two input shapes — here is the contrast.

blocks.text: Pass a Python list to `pd.Series()` and the index defaults to 0, 1, …, n−1. Pass a dict and the dict's keys become the index labels. `pd.Series([18, 20, 22, 22, 26, 28, 80])` gives index 0–6; `pd.Series({"Lagos": 18, "Abuja": 20, "Kano": 22})` gives city-name labels.

Pass a dict of equal-length lists to `pd.DataFrame()` and each key becomes a column name. `pd.DataFrame({"order_id": [1001, 1002, 1003], "city": ["Lagos", "Abuja", "Kano"], "delivery_time_minutes": [18, 20, 22]})` builds a three-column, three-row orders table.

remediation_steps.title: read_csv vs read_excel — which file, which function
remediation_steps.lede: The file extension tells you which reader to call.

blocks.text: `pd.read_csv()` is the main pandas function for reading a delimited text file — such as a CSV — into a DataFrame. `pd.read_excel()` reads an Excel file (such as a .xlsx workbook) into a DataFrame. Use `read_csv` for `orders.csv`; use `read_excel` for `orders.xlsx`.

remediation_steps.title: Key arguments: path, sheet_name, and sep
remediation_steps.lede: Three arguments cover the most common reading scenarios.

blocks.text: `read_csv()` takes the file path (or URL) as its first argument. `read_excel()` additionally takes `sheet_name` to choose which sheet to load — that is why `pd.read_excel("orders.xlsx", sheet_name="January")` names the sheet but `pd.read_csv("orders.csv")` does not need to. `read_csv()` also accepts `sep` to change the delimiter: `pd.read_csv("orders.csv", sep=";")` handles a semicolon-delimited export.
